summary: Gives sample inputs and expected outputs for HMAC built with the MD5 and SHA-1 hash functions. Implementers can run these test cases to check that their code computes message authentication codes correctly. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2202 provides known key and message pairs with the results for keyed-hash message authentication (HMAC). Developers can compare their output with these cases to check whether their implementation behaves as expected.

questions: what are the hmac md5 test cases
subtitle: Test cases with expected results for HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA-1 implementations.

tldr.problem: Implementers need known inputs and expected outputs to compare their HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA-1 code with other implementations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC supplies test cases containing a key, data and expected digest for each HMAC construction. It also includes truncated digest results for cases that demonstrate truncation.
tldr.outcome: The test cases are intended for conformance testing and interoperability checks. The RFC cautions that matching the results is not a claim of absolute correctness relative to the HMAC definition.

today: RFC 2202 is an Informational memo that publishes test cases for HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA-1. The batch metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Purpose of the Test Cases
sections.content:
RFC 2202 gives two sets of test cases: one for HMAC-MD5 and one for HMAC-SHA-1. HMAC uses a hash function to create a message authentication code, and the RFC notes that both constructions are used by IPsec and other protocols.

The test cases are intended as conformance tests. Results were cross-checked by three independent implementations, but the authors do not claim that agreement proves absolute correctness against the HMAC definition.
sections.plainLanguage: The test cases provide known answers for two HMAC variants. Matching those answers helps show that separate implementations produce the same results.

sections.title: Inputs and Expected Digests
sections.content:
Each case gives a key, data and expected digest. Keys and data may be written as hexadecimal values beginning with 0x or as quoted ASCII strings. For an ASCII string, the HMAC input does not include a trailing null character.

The HMAC-MD5 section and HMAC-SHA-1 section provide corresponding cases with different key and data forms. Some cases use repeated byte values or keys longer than a hash block, and each section includes a case with a truncated digest.
sections.plainLanguage: For each case, give the stated key and data to the implementation and compare its result with the listed digest. Quoted text is used as written, without an extra ending null character.

sections.title: Digest Truncation
sections.content:
The introduction explains that when an HMAC output is truncated, the more significant bits are retained. In network byte order, these are the bits on the left. The test cases that show a shortened result let implementers compare this behavior as well as the full digest.

The RFC points to RFC 2104 for the HMAC construction and its discussion of truncation. It does not restate the complete construction in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: When a shorter digest is needed, keep its leftmost bits. The shortened test results show what an implementation should return for the listed cases.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says that this document raises no security issues. It refers readers to RFC 2104 for discussion of the strength of the HMAC construction.

These vectors test outputs; they are not a broader security assessment of an implementation or deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo provides test data, not a full security review. It points to RFC 2104 for discussion of HMAC strength.

references.text: Krawczyk, H., Bellare, M., and R. Canetti, "HMAC: Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication", RFC 2104, February 1997.
Rivest, R., "The MD5 Message-Digest Algorithm", RFC 1321, April 1992.
Oehler, M., and R. Glenn, "HMAC-MD5 IP Authentication with Replay Prevention", RFC 2085, February 1997.
